titulo: Three things you must do before you fly
subtitulo: The only part of this course with a deadline — your passport, your cover and your phone

steps.pt: Part 2A. This is the one part of the course with a clock on it — everything here has to happen before you leave the house, and one item on the list cannot be fixed at the airport. Three things: your passport, your cover, your phone. Before we start, ten seconds of warm-up, because it's the habit everything else sits on. Hand flat on your thigh, one tap per syllable, all the same size: Bar-ce-lo-na. Four taps, four equal taps. And keep the vowels flat — say it, don't slide it. Right. Thing one.

Your passport — and this is the one that can cost you the whole trip. If you're British, it has to pass two tests, not one. Test one: it was issued less than ten years before the day you arrive. Test two: it's still valid for at least three months after the day you leave. Almost everybody knows the second and almost nobody knows the first. Here's the trap: passports issued between 2018 and 2020 could carry over up to nine extra months from the old one. So a passport that cheerfully says 'valid until 2027' may have been issued in 2016 — and it fails. And it doesn't fail at the Spanish border. It fails at your own check-in desk, at home, with the flight and the hotel already paid for. Go and get it. Look at both dates. Now, not tonight.

Bought your trip three weeks out? There's time. Booked it last night? There's time for the essentials — but not for a passport. Renewals are measured in weeks, not days, and the urgent appointments go first. So the order is: passport today, the rest of the list this week. And if both dates pass, tick it off, put it back in the drawer and never think about it again. Americans, same drill, one test instead of two: at least three months of validity beyond the day you leave Europe.

George here, with the one that turns up in your inbox looking official. ETIAS. You may have read that Europe is bringing in a twenty-euro travel authorisation. It's true that it's coming. It is not true that you can get one now: as of the summer of 2026 there is no application portal open. None. So if a website offers to sell you an ETIAS today — service fee, reassuring green tick, urgent countdown — it is a scam, and there is an entire industry of them. There is one official site, it's run by the European Union, and it isn't taking applications. Nothing to do today. Check the official page about sixty days before you fly.

Thing two: cover. If you're British, the GHIC card is worth having — it gets you state healthcare in Spain on the same terms as a Spaniard, which is often free. What it will not do is fly you home in an air ambulance or pay a private hospital, and the Costa del Sol is stuffed with private hospitals with English signs on the door. So: GHIC gets you treated, insurance gets you home. They are not the same product and you want both. If you're American, this stops being advice and becomes a prerequisite — there is no reciprocal health agreement between the United States and Spain, your home policy very probably covers nothing there, and hospitals routinely ask non-residents to pay up front. Buy the policy before you fly, and put the emergency number in your phone, not in a drawer.

Thing three: your phone — and this is where the internet will happily sell you something you may not need. Before you buy anything, open your own network's app and search 'roaming'. If you're on O2, most plans still include Europe with no daily charge: buy nothing. Vodafone, EE and Three mostly add a couple of pounds a day, automatically, whether you want it or not — two of you, fourteen days, and you've quietly spent about fifty-six pounds. That's when a travel eSIM pays for itself. Americans: same homework, and anyone quoting you a flat price for a US carrier package is guessing. And if you do buy an eSIM, install it and test it at home, on your own wifi. Activating one needs internet, and you will be landing without any. The classic disaster is buying it on the plane while it's taxiing and discovering in the arrivals hall that your handset is locked.

And if you land with nothing — no eSIM, roaming off, and a plan that turns out to cover Andorra but not Spain — you walk into a phone shop and buy a Spanish prepaid SIM. One thing to know before you do: Spain registers prepaid SIMs against a document, and they want the physical passport in their hand. A photo of it on your screen usually gets refused. So: passport out. Then these words.
Do you have prepaid SIM cards?

Do I need my passport? — and listen to that 'c': neh-THEH-see-toh. That's the 'th' of 'think', and it's the sound that says Spain rather than Mexico.

steps.promptPt: He's started typing. You want to know whether to dig the passport out from the bottom of the bag now or not. Ask him. Say it now.
steps.pt: Do I need my passport?

steps.es: Sí, el original. Una foto no me vale.
steps.pinyin: see, el oh-ree-khee-NAL. OO-nah FOH-toh noh meh BAH-leh
steps.pt: 👂 'Yes — the real one. A photo is no good.' — a Spanish prepaid SIM is registered against the document in your hand.

steps.pt: George again, with the word you're about to get wrong and then say twenty more times this trip: móvil. Mobile. Two English habits, both fatal. First: there is no V in Spain. The letter is on the page, the sound isn't — it's a B. MOH-beel. Second: look at the little mark over the O. That isn't decoration, it's the loudspeaker — it tells you exactly where the punch lands. MOH-beel, not mo-VEEL. And while I'm here: datos. DAH-tohs. Not 'DAY-tuz'. Every vowel gets paid in Spanish. None of them work for free.

steps.pt: Can you activate it for me here, please? — again, no V: ak-tee-BAR, fah-BOR.
steps.tts: ¿Me la puede activar aquí, por favor?

steps.promptPt: He's handing you the card in its little envelope and looking at the next customer. You are not walking out of here with a card that isn't switched on. Ask him to activate it right here. Say it now.

steps.promptPt: Different shop, different assistant, and she's already opening a monthly contract on the screen. Say the one line that stops it — prepaid, data only. Say it now.

Two things in focus. First, a shape you've just used without noticing: '¿Me la puede activar?' — can you activate it for me. That '¿Me lo puede…?', '¿Me la puede…?' is a workhorse you'll reuse all trip: ¿Me lo puede escribir? — can you write it down for me. ¿Me la puede activar? — can you activate it for me. Don't learn the endings tonight; learn the shape. Second, the fourth item on the list, which isn't a phrase at all: if you're taking a fast train — Madrid to Seville, Barcelona to Valencia — buy it sixty to ninety days out. Spanish high-speed fares climb steeply as the date closes in, and the cheap Ouigo and Avlo seats go first. It's the only booking on this list that gets more expensive while you think about it.

Part 2A done, and notice it was a checklist, not a lesson: both passport dates checked, cover bought, phone sorted and tested at home, nobody sold you an ETIAS, and a train ticket in the diary. Next, part 2B: you've landed. The camera, the four fingerprints and the three questions at the border. And one last thing, because this is the corner of the course with the shortest shelf life — rules change. Check the official page before you fly; the link is in the app.

secoes.titulo: The passport: two dates, not one
secoes.corpo: For British passport holders travelling to Spain, the document must satisfy BOTH conditions at once: issued less than 10 years before the date you arrive, AND valid for at least 3 months after the day you leave the Schengen area. The reason so many people get caught is that passports issued between 2018 and 2020 could inherit up to 9 months from the previous document — so the expiry date printed inside can be perfectly fine while the issue date silently fails. You'll be refused at your departure airport, not at the Spanish border, which means the airline is under no obligation to refund anything. Check both dates today; renewals take weeks.

secoes.titulo: GHIC treats you. Insurance gets you home.
secoes.corpo: The UK GHIC gives British visitors medically necessary state healthcare in Spain on the same terms as a Spanish resident — emergency care, sudden illness, pre-existing conditions included. It does not cover repatriation, private hospitals or anything non-medical, and the UK government says explicitly that it is not a substitute for travel insurance. In the British-heavy stretches of the Costa del Sol, the clinic with the English sign is very often private, where the GHIC is worth nothing — which is why the single most valuable question in part 8A is '¿Esto es público o privado?'. American travellers have no equivalent card at all: there is no reciprocal health agreement between the US and Spain, and hospitals commonly ask non-residents to pay up front.

secoes.titulo: Roaming: check before you buy anything
secoes.corpo: British networks diverge sharply and change with each new plan generation, so the only reliable move is to open your own network's app and read your plan. As a rough map for 2026: O2 still includes EU roaming with no daily fee on most contract plans (fair use around 25 GB); Vodafone lets most plans use the UK allowance across Europe but applies a daily charge on many of them; EE sells a Roam Abroad daily pass; Three's Go Roam coverage varies by plan and has been revised. Daily charges apply automatically — there is no opt-out once you use the phone abroad. Two travellers × 14 days × £2/day ≈ £56, which is where a travel eSIM starts to make sense. If your network is O2, buy nothing.

secoes.titulo: Why they want the physical passport for a SIM card
secoes.corpo: Spanish prepaid SIMs must be registered to an identity document at the point of sale, and shops routinely refuse a photo or a scan on your phone — Vodafone and Movistar counters are reported to be the strictest. Take the passport itself. This is also the reason a travel eSIM bought and tested at home is the calmer option: it needs no counter, no queue and no document, but it does need an internet connection to activate, which you won't have until you're through the airport.

secoes.titulo: ETIAS: nothing to buy, nothing to do
secoes.corpo: ETIAS is the European travel authorisation that has been announced, priced at €20, and repeatedly postponed. As of July 2026 there is no open application portal, and press reports suggest a further slip into 2027 that the Commission has not confirmed. There is exactly one official website, run by the EU. Any site charging you a 'processing fee' for an ETIAS today is selling a document that does not yet exist. Check the official page about 60 days before you travel and take whatever it says then over whatever you read here.

_cena_pendente: NÃO DECLARADA DE PROPÓSITO. A frase está escrita e conferida contra o SCHEMA §6 — «The flight is paid for, the passport is in the drawer with two dates in it, and the only person who will ever compare them is standing at your own check-in desk, with a queue behind you.» — mas declarar `cena` põe a parte EM VIGOR, e medido em 28/07/2026 isso deposita 12 erros duros na build: G4 média 610 chars/clipe (teto 120) · G4b 10 de 10 clipes de narração acima de 320 (389 a 865) · G15 a parte ensina molde e nunca o NOMEIA («a shape you've just used», nunca «the frame»). Os doze só saem reescrevendo narração já gravada — os 10 mp3 estão em static/audio e no manifesto, e valida-audio.mjs roda em modo estrito no prebuild: mexer no texto acusa «TEXTO À FRENTE DO ÁUDIO» até regravar. É reuso integral por decisão da grade, então o número foi reportado em vez de forçado. Trocar esta chave por `cena` no dia em que a narração for repartida e regravada.
_clique_nao_se_aplica: B04 NÃO é casa de molde nenhum: moldes.json dá ME-PUEDE à casa B03 e lista B04 entre os redisparos, e por isso a raiz não declara `moldes`. PRODUTO T4 é explícito — o slot do bloco final só é ocupado pelo clique «quando a parte declara `moldes`»; sem isso ele é «Gramática em foco», que é exatamente o que e02a-n09 é. Além da lei: ME-PUEDE serve UMA vez nesta parte (e02a-p04), então uma contagem honesta de ≥3 lugares é aritmeticamente impossível aqui — e o mp3 de e02a-n09 não contém contagem, nem desconto, nem piso. O `clique` que existia neste arquivo declarava três lugares para um molde que pagou em um, e apontava cliqueAudioKey para um clipe que não diz nada daquilo. Removido por ser declaração sem áudio. Se um dia B04 virar casa de molde, o clique volta com a contagem do que o aluno de fato fez aqui.
permissao: You do not have to buy anything for your phone. Open your own network's app, search roaming and read what your plan already includes — if Europe is in there, the right move is to spend nothing. And there is no ETIAS to buy today, whatever a website tells you.
frasePiso: You will get on the plane with a passport nobody can turn back, cover that pays, and a phone that works when you land. Most people who fly to Spain check one date out of two and find out at the desk.
espelho: Turning your phone round to show a photo of your passport is the bit that reads as odd there. At home the picture is proof enough; at a Spanish counter the document has to be in the assistant's hand, or the sale stops.

fichasCulturais.sinal: The assistant stops typing, puts his hand out and waits — and when you show him the photo of your passport on your screen he shakes his head and the card goes back in the drawer.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: He does not trust me. A photo is a photo. This is either bureaucracy for its own sake or he has decided I am not worth the trouble.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: A Spanish prepaid SIM is registered against an identity document at the point of sale, and the shop carries the record — so the assistant needs the document itself in his hand, not an image of it. Vodafone and Movistar counters are reported as the strictest (docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §8.3).
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Have the physical passport out of the bag before you reach the counter, and ask him straight out whether he needs it: ¿Necesito el pasaporte?
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You leave the arrivals hall with a working number in the time it takes him to type, instead of going back for the document you left in the case.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not for a travel eSIM you bought before you flew, and not at a hotel desk asking for the wifi — there nobody registers anything and no document changes hands.
